'''''Securigera varia''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Coronilla varia'''''), commonly known as '''crownvetch'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SEVA4|taxon=Securigera varia|access-date=8 November 2015}}</ref> or '''purple crown vetch''', is a low-growing [[legume]] vine. It is native to [[Africa]], [[Asia]] and [[Europe]] and is commonly used throughout the [[United States]] and [[Canada]] for [[erosion control]], roadside planting and [[soil rehabilitation]]. It has become an [[invasive species]] in many states of the US.

Crownvetch grows {{convert|1 to 2 |ft|m}} feet tall and bears small clusters of {{convert|1/2|inch|mm}} pink and white [[flower]]s from early summer to late fall. The variety Penngift produces mounds of pink flowers. Crownvetch is a tough, aggressive spreading plant that will crowd out its neighbors in a show garden but is well suited to a sunny bank, where it will grow for decades with little to no fertilizing, mowing, or weeding since the thick foliage prevents other weeds.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=OSC Seeds. (n.d.).|title=Crownvetch.|url=http://www.oscseeds.com/ecommerce/-ground--cover-seed/Crownvetch.htm|access-date=2014-11-27|archive-date=2014-12-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205153814/http://www.oscseeds.com/ecommerce/-ground--cover-seed/Crownvetch.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Its deep, tenacious, complex root system<ref name="multiple">Gustine, D. L., & Moyer, B. G. (1990). Crownvetch (Coronilla varia L.). In Legumes and Oilseed Crops I (pp. 341-354). Springer Berlin Heidelberg.</ref> and thick, fern-like leaves provide excellent [[erosion]] control where it is used as a ground cover. However, this legume has a very long [[germination period]] of about 6 months and does not create full coverage until two or three years later.<ref name="multiple"/>

==Taxonomy==
''Securigera varia'' was given its first scientific description in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] with the name ''Coronilla varia''. In 1989 Per Lassen proposed moving it to the genus ''[[Securigera]]'',<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |id=487281-1 |title=''Coronilla varia'' L. |access-date=3 May 2024}}</ref> which had been created by [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in 1805.<ref>{{cite POWO |id=331950-2 |title=''Securigera'' DC. |access-date=3 May 2024}}</ref>

{{As of|2024}} the correct classification of the species is uncertain. In databases like [[Plants of the World Online]],<ref name="POWO" /> [[World Flora Online]],<ref>{{Cite WFO |title=''Coronilla varia'' L. |id=0000213691 |access-date=3 May 2024}}</ref> and the Legume Data Portal,<ref>{{cite web |title=''Coronilla varia'' L. |url=https://hp-legume.gbif-staging.org/taxonomy/taxon/2738047 |website=Legume Data Portal |publisher=Legume Phylogeny Working Group (LPWG) |access-date=3 May 2024}}</ref> ''Coronilla varia'' is listed as the accepted name. On the other hand ''Securigera varia'' is listed as the accepted name in resources such as Flora of the Southeastern United States,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Weakley |first1=A.S. |last2=Southeastern Flora Team |title=''Securigera varia'' detail |url=https://fsus.ncbg.unc.edu/main.php?pg=show-taxon-detail.php&lsid=urn:lsid:ncbg.unc.edu:taxon:{F7C8EE8B-5B46-4823-9028-E2C13BE1B04D} |website=Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS) |access-date=3 May 2024 |date=2024}}</ref> World Plants,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=Michael |title=Synonymic Checklist and Distribution of the World Flora. Version 19.2 |url=https://www.worldplants.de |website=World Plants |access-date=3 May 2024 |date=17 April 2024}}</ref> and the New Zealand Organisms Register.<ref>{{cite web |last1=New Zealand Organisms Register |title=NZOR Name Details - ''Securigera varia'' (L.) Lassen |url=https://www.nzor.org.nz/names/6317a3cf-5557-41e9-bcf6-9534150d641a |website=NZOR |access-date=3 May 2024 |date=2024}}</ref>

==Forage==
Crownvetch is toxic to [[horse]]s and other non-[[ruminant]]s because of the presence of [[Glycosylamine|nitroglycosides]]. If consumed in large amounts, it can stunt growth, or even lead to [[paralysis]] and death. However, this is not true for ruminant animals such as cattle, goats, and sheep.<ref name="moyer"/> These aliphatic nitro compounds are degraded in ruminant digestion and do not affect the animals.<ref name="moyer">{{cite journal | last1 = Moyer | first1 = BG | last2 = Gustine | first2 = DL | year = 1984 | title = Regeneration of Coronilla varia L. (crownvetch) plants from callus culture | journal = Journal of Plant Biotechnology | volume = 3 | issue = 2| pages = 143–148 | doi=10.1007/BF00033735| s2cid = 26268447 }}</ref>

Crownvetch was originally labeled as a poor forage for farm animals but more recently it has been deemed as a good forage when fed as hay to or grazed by ruminants.<ref>Burns JC, Cope WA. 1974. Nutritive Value of Crownvetch Forage as Influenced by Structural Constituents and Phenolic and Tannin Compounds. Agronomy Journal, 66, p 195-200. Retrieved from https://www.agronomy.org/publications/aj/abstracts/66/2/AJ0660020195</ref> It consists of 21.7% crude protein and 22.2% crude fibre.<ref name="reynolds"/> In an experiment involving the digestibility of crownvetch in sheep, it was found that the crude protein is 65.6% and the crude fibre is 46.2% digestible which is similar, but slightly less than the digestibility of alfalfa forage.<ref name="reynolds">Reynolds PJ, Jackson C, Lindahl IL, Henson PR. 1967. Consumption and Digestibility of Crownvetch (Coronilla varia L.) Forage by Sheep. Agronomy Journal, 59, p 589-591. Retrieved from https://dl.sciencesocieties.org/publications/aj/abstracts/59/6/AJ0590060589</ref> As previously mentioned, this only applies to ruminant animals as it is toxic to non-ruminants.<ref name="moyer"/>

Crownvetch has been identified as an invasive in several midwestern states. It is very hard to eradicate once established.<ref>[http://www.in.gov/dnr/files/Crown_vetch.pdf Indiana Dept of Natural Resources]</ref>

It is also a common host-plant for the moth ''[[Zygaena ephialtes]].''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266205205|title=Habitat requirements of conspicuous burnet moth Zygaena ephialtes (Linnaeus, 1767; Lepidoptera: Zygaenidae) (PDF Download Available)|website=ResearchGate|language=en|access-date=2017-11-16}}</ref>
